answers.answer: Replication copies data changes between servers; each maintained copy is a replica. Partitioning/sharding divides data into groups instead of making copies of the same data; each group can itself have replicas. Copies can serve reads and take over server responsibilities, but routing and safe takeover require separate work, lag permits old reads, and copies do not automatically add write capacity. A new replica starts with a snapshot at a known point, then receives ordered change-log records and applies them. The log records later source changes; applying updates the replica data so queries see the change. Snapshot and log position must agree to avoid missing or incorrectly applying changes. Receiving alone does not establish application or read visibility.

evidence.quote: Copies data changes between servers. Each maintained copy is a replica.
Read routing and a safe takeover process are separate design work; a second copy does not configure either automatically.
Adding read replicas can increase read capacity. It does not automatically increase the number of writes the system can handle.
Solve different problems. Replication keeps copies of the same data. Sharding divides data into different groups. A system can use both by keeping several copies of each group.
A copy of the database at a known point. A common replication setup starts with this copy.

Records later changes on the source. The replica receives these records and applies them while preserving the required source order. Applying an older change after a newer dependent change could restore an out-of-date value.
The initial copy and starting log position must agree. Otherwise the handoff can miss changes or apply them incorrectly. Each replication implementation coordinates that boundary.
The replica updated its data so queries can see the change.

answers.answer: Asynchronous replication lets the writing server report success before a replica confirms; acknowledgement means only the configured success condition was met. If it acknowledges, permanently fails before sending the change, and a replica is promoted, that replica lacks the acknowledged write. Avoiding the replica wait reduces write waiting but allows old reads and recent-write loss. Synchronous replication waits for required replica confirmations: specify the set or count and whether confirmation means received (possibly in memory), durably stored (survives restart), or applied (query-visible). Durable acknowledgements protect against loss of the writing server but add delay; too few responding required replicas can stall writes. Synchronous success need not involve every replica or make every replica read current. It does not protect against losing every copy or accidental logical changes.

evidence.quote: The writing server can acknowledge success before a replica confirms the change. Acknowledgement means the configured success condition was met, not that every copy has the data.
If the writing server fails permanently before sending a confirmed change, a replacement replica will not have that change.
The trade-off is less waiting during writes, in exchange for older reads and possible loss of recent writes during failover.
A write waits for confirmation from the required replicas before reporting success. What that confirmation means matters.
The replica has the change, possibly only in memory.
The replica saved it to storage that can survive a restart.
The replica updated its data so queries can see the change.
Waiting for durable copies protects against losing the writing server. It adds delay, and writes can stall if too few required replicas respond.
Choose the required replica set or count and acknowledgement stage. This protects against specified failures, not loss of every copy or accidental logical changes.
Synchronous replication does not necessarily wait for every replica. Nor does every synchronous mode guarantee that replica reads already show the change.

answers.answer: Lag means a replica is behind receiving or applying source changes. A successful write can be absent from a replica read because it has not been applied, even if received. Read-your-writes means later reads include your completed change or newer state. Reading the authoritative primary holding the write avoids waiting for replica application but concentrates load and requires correct authority after failover. Waiting for evidence that the chosen replica applied that exact write permits that replica to serve the fresh read but adds delay and can fail; fixed sleeps and average lag are insufficient proof. Accepting stale reads suits delay-tolerant work and permits replica reads without that freshness wait, but gives no read-your-writes guarantee. Routing cannot recover a write already lost in failover; precise latency figures are unsupported. A leader accepts writes: a single leader orders writes for a dataset and followers copy them, requiring failover on replacement. Multiple leaders accept and exchange writes, potentially nearby, but independent edits need conflict rules and latest-timestamp selection can discard valid edits. Leaderless requests go through any coordinator to the data replicas, wait for configured reply counts, and need difference repair and concurrent-version reconciliation. More write entry points do not guarantee conflict freedom or one current value, and topology alone does not determine sync versus async.

evidence.quote: A replica is behind the source in receiving or applying changes. State which stage a lag measurement describes; data received but not applied is not yet visible to reads.
Later reads include your own completed change or newer state. Read from the authoritative primary holding the write, or wait for evidence that the selected replica applied that specific change.
Primary reads concentrate load and require correct authority after failover. Waiting for a replica adds delay and can fail. Routing alone cannot recover a write already lost during failover.
A fixed sleep or low average lag is not proof that a particular write is visible.

Delay-tolerant reads can use replicas. Freshness-sensitive reads need suitable routing or progress checks. Waiting for durable replica acknowledgements narrows some loss windows but adds commit delay and dependence on those replicas.
One server accepts writes for a set of data. Followers copy its changes. This gives writes one place to be ordered, but replacing that leader requires a failover process.

Several servers accept writes and exchange changes. This can let users write to a nearby server. If two leaders change the same item independently, the system needs a conflict rule. Choosing the latest timestamp can discard another valid edit.

Requests can go through any coordinating server, which sends them to the replicas holding the data. The system waits for a configured number of replies and repairs differences between copies. Concurrent versions still need reconciliation; no topology name guarantees one current value or conflict-free updates.
These arrangements describe where writes go. They do not, by themselves, tell you whether replication is synchronous or asynchronous.

answers.answer: Failover transfers failed-server responsibilities; promotion makes a suitable replica the leader. Split brain means two servers both act as sole leader and can accept conflicting changes. Silence may mean a broken network while the old leader still writes. Select a suitable replacement whose progress meets acceptable recent-write loss, fence the old leader by shutdown or blocked access, promote the replacement and redirect application connections. Exact eligibility checks and implementation mechanics are not supplied. An asynchronous acknowledged write can be absent from the replacement and lost. A healthy current replica can faithfully apply an accidental deletion, so it need not restore earlier data. Backups preserve an earlier recoverable state; point-in-time recovery restores a backup and replays saved logs up to a chosen moment before the deletion. Retention and available logs limit history. Restore tests must demonstrate usable application data and measure recovery duration; an untested backup or current replica alone proves neither required recovery time nor recoverable history.

evidence.quote: Moves a failed server's responsibilities to another server. In a single-leader system, the process selects a suitable replica, promotes it to leader, and redirects application connections. How current that replica is affects whether recent writes survive.
A missing response does not prove the old leader stopped. Its network connection can be broken while it still accepts writes.
Happens when two servers both act as the sole leader. They can accept conflicting changes.
Prevents the old leader from continuing to write, for example by shutting it down or blocking its access.
If the writing server fails permanently before sending a confirmed change, a replacement replica will not have that change.
Replication also copies unwanted changes. If someone deletes the wrong records, replicas can apply that deletion too.
Preserves an earlier recoverable state.
Restores a backup and replays saved change logs up to a chosen moment. That can recover the database to just before an accidental deletion.
Retention and available logs bound recoverable history. Restore tests must reconstruct usable application data and measure how long recovery takes; file existence alone proves neither.

answers.answer: Provisional policy: use a single writer with replicas, require durable replica acknowledgements to narrow confirmed-write loss from writer failure, route delay-tolerant reports to replicas, and route freshness-sensitive reads to the authoritative primary or wait for proof the selected replica applied the relevant change. First establish allowed acknowledged-write loss, report staleness, commit delay and recovery downtime, plus the failures to withstand; the question does not justify an exact replica count or numerical targets. Configure the required replica set/count to those failures and accept that missing required confirmations may stall writes. On failure choose a suitable sufficiently current replica, fence the old leader, promote and redirect clients. Maintain backups and retained logs for historical recovery, because replication copies accidental deletions. Monitor replication progress, stage-specific lag, health and write waits; exercise failover and restore usable application data while measuring recovery time against targets and checking retention/log coverage. Copies cost storage, network and operations. Replication alone specifies neither acknowledgements nor safe takeover: asynchronous confirmations can be lost, durable synchronous writes depend on reachable required copies, and losing all copies or propagating unwanted changes remains possible. Therefore zero loss and uninterrupted writes cannot be promised from the label alone.

evidence.quote: Choose acceptable acknowledged-write loss, read freshness, write latency and recovery time before choosing replica settings.

Delay-tolerant reads can use replicas. Freshness-sensitive reads need suitable routing or progress checks. Waiting for durable replica acknowledgements narrows some loss windows but adds commit delay and dependence on those replicas.
Choose the required replica set or count and acknowledgement stage. This protects against specified failures, not loss of every copy or accidental logical changes.
Safe failover needs protection against the old leader continuing to write, not just a replacement server.
Replication helps keep service running after a server failure. Backups and retained logs help recover earlier data.
Retention and available logs bound recoverable history. Restore tests must reconstruct usable application data and measure how long recovery takes; file existence alone proves neither.
Copies consume storage, network and operating work. Monitor replication progress, lag, health and write waits; exercise failover and historical restore against the required recovery targets.
During a network split, operations that need agreement with unreachable copies must wait or fail. Independent operation instead needs explicit handling of old reads and conflicting writes.
